distractors.A: The Pricing Calculator only estimates Azure service costs; it does not capture on-premises costs for comparison.
distractors.C: Service Health reports Azure service outages and maintenance, not cost comparisons.
distractors.D: Cost Management reports on money already spent in Azure, not an on-premises vs Azure comparison.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Compare on-premises vs Azure' = TCO Calculator.

references: Azure TCO Calculator

questions.stem: After months of running Azure workloads, finance wants to analyze actual spending and see which service costs the most. Which tool should they open?

explanation.correct: Microsoft Cost Management provides cost analysis of actual billed usage, letting you break spend down by service, resource group, or tag.

distractors.B: The TCO Calculator compares on-premises and Azure costs; it does not analyze your live Azure bill.
distractors.C: Azure Policy enforces resource rules; it does not report spending.
distractors.D: The Pricing Calculator produces pre-deployment estimates, not reports of real spending.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Analyze actual/real spend' = Microsoft Cost Management.

references: Microsoft Cost Management

questions.stem: An administrator wants an automatic email when subscription spending reaches a set percentage of the monthly limit. What should they configure in Cost Management?

options.text: A budget with an alert threshold

explanation.correct: In Microsoft Cost Management you create a budget and set alert thresholds that email recipients when spending approaches the defined limit.

distractors.B: Azure Policy controls which resources can be deployed, not spending alerts.
distractors.C: A resource lock prevents deletion or changes to a resource; it has nothing to do with spending notifications.
distractors.D: Service Health alerts notify you about Azure service issues, not your budget.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Notify at a spending threshold' = Cost Management budget + alert.

references: Microsoft Cost Management

questions.stem: Two identical virtual machines are priced differently on the Pricing Calculator. Which factor most likely explains the difference?

options.text: The Azure region each VM is deployed to
The resource group each VM sits in
The tags applied to each VM
The display name given to each VM

explanation.correct: Prices for the same resource vary by region because of differing datacenter and operating costs, so region is a genuine cost factor.

distractors.B: Placing a resource in a different resource group does not change its price; resource groups are free containers.
distractors.C: Tags are billing and organization labels; applying them does not change a resource's price.
distractors.D: A resource's name is free metadata and never changes its price.

explanation.exam_pattern: Same resource, different price = region is the usual cause.

references: Azure cost factors

questions.stem: A solution moves large amounts of data in and out of an Azure region. Which data transfer typically appears as a charge on the bill?

options.text: Inbound data uploaded into the Azure region
Outbound data leaving the Azure region to the internet
A VM reading from its own attached OS disk
Data written to a managed disk in the same region

explanation.correct: Outbound (egress) data transfer leaving an Azure datacenter or region is generally billed, which is why high outbound traffic raises costs.

distractors.A: Inbound (ingress) data into an Azure datacenter is generally free.
distractors.C: A VM reading its own OS disk is not internet data transfer and is not billed as egress.
distractors.D: Writing to a disk in the same region is storage activity, not billed internet egress.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ingress usually free, egress usually billed.

references: Azure cost factors

questions.stem: A company wants its Azure bill broken down by department so each team's spend is visible. What should they apply to resources?

explanation.correct: Tags are name/value pairs (such as Department:Finance) attached to resources; Cost Management can then group and filter spending by tag.

distractors.A: Resource locks prevent deletion or changes; they do not categorize costs.
distractors.B: Azure Policy enforces configuration rules; it does not break the bill down by team.
distractors.D: RBAC assignments control who can access resources, not how costs are grouped.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Group or track cost by team or project' = tags.

references: Azure resource tags

questions.stem: To cut costs, an admin stops (deallocates) a development VM every night. For the hours it is deallocated, what is still billed?

options.text: Its virtual CPU and memory compute

explanation.correct: Deallocating a VM stops compute (vCPU/RAM) billing, but the managed disks that store the VM stay provisioned and keep incurring storage charges.

distractors.A: Compute billing stops while a VM is deallocated, so vCPU and memory is exactly what you are no longer paying for.
distractors.C: Charges continue for the disks regardless of licensing; an OS license alone does not describe the ongoing cost.
distractors.D: Storage for the VM's disks persists and is still billed, so leaving a deallocated VM in place is not free.

explanation.exam_pattern: Deallocated VM = no compute charge, but disks still cost.

references: Azure cost factors

questions.stem: A production database VM runs 24/7 with steady, predictable usage for the next three years. Which option most reduces its compute cost?

options.text: Switch it to Azure Spot capacity

explanation.correct: Azure Reservations give a discount in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment, which suits steady, always-on workloads with predictable usage.

distractors.A: Azure Spot offers deep discounts but can be evicted at any time, so it is unsuitable for an always-on production database.
distractors.C: Pay-as-you-go carries no commitment discount, so it is the more expensive option for steady long-term usage.
distractors.D: A resource lock protects against deletion or changes and has no effect on price.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Steady, long-term, predictable' + save money = Reservations.

references: Azure Reservations

questions.stem: An architect must choose between Premium SSD and Standard HDD managed disks. Regarding cost, which statement is correct?

options.text: Standard HDD costs more because it is an older technology
Disk tier never affects price, only region does
The higher-performance Premium SSD tier costs more than Standard HDD
Both disk tiers cost exactly the same

explanation.correct: Resource type and performance tier are cost factors; higher-performance Premium SSD disks are priced above lower-performance Standard HDD disks.

distractors.A: Standard HDD is the lower-cost tier, not the more expensive one.
distractors.B: Both tier and region affect price; tier is a real cost factor, not irrelevant.
distractors.D: Different performance tiers are priced differently, so they are not the same cost.

explanation.exam_pattern: Higher performance tier/SKU = higher price.

references: Azure cost factors

questions.stem: A colleague treats the figure from the Pricing Calculator as the exact amount the company will be invoiced. Why is that assumption wrong?

options.text: The Pricing Calculator only works after resources are deployed
It is a planning estimate; the real charge depends on actual usage
The Pricing Calculator reports last month's invoice totals
The Pricing Calculator always overstates cost by design

explanation.correct: The Pricing Calculator produces an estimate from the configuration you enter; the actual bill reflects real consumption and is tracked in Cost Management.

distractors.A: It is a pre-deployment planning tool and does not require any resources to exist.
distractors.C: It does not read invoices; reviewing actual billed amounts is the job of Cost Management.
distractors.D: The calculator is neither deliberately high nor low; it estimates from your inputs, which may differ from real usage.

explanation.exam_pattern: Pricing Calculator = estimate; Cost Management = actual spend.

references: Azure Pricing Calculator

questions.stem: Under Azure's pay-as-you-go model, what most directly determines the size of a workload's monthly compute bill?

options.text: How much the resources are actually used
The color theme set in the Azure portal

explanation.correct: Pay-as-you-go is consumption-based billing: you are charged for the resources you actually use, so usage is the main cost driver.

distractors.B: Tags are free labels for organization and reporting; they do not drive the bill.
distractors.C: Resource groups are free logical containers and do not themselves generate charges.
distractors.D: Portal appearance settings have no effect on billing.

explanation.exam_pattern: Consumption / pay-as-you-go = you pay for what you use.

references: Azure cost factors

questions.stem: A manager wants to be warned specifically about an unexpected spike in Azure spending. Which service provides that alert?

explanation.correct: Cost Management provides cost alerts (including anomaly and budget alerts) that warn you when spending behaves unexpectedly or crosses a threshold.

distractors.B: Service Health alerts cover Azure service outages and maintenance, not your spending.
distractors.C: Advisor offers improvement recommendations, including some cost tips, but is not the spending-spike alerting tool.
distractors.D: Application Insights monitors application performance, not costs.

explanation.exam_pattern: Spending alerts come from Cost Management, not Service Health.

references: Microsoft Cost Management

questions.stem: An organization must guarantee that resources are only ever created in approved Azure regions. Which service enforces this rule automatically?

explanation.correct: Azure Policy evaluates resources against rules and can deny deployments that violate them, such as creating a resource in a non-approved region.

distractors.B: The Service Trust Portal hosts Microsoft's compliance reports; it does not enforce your deployment rules.
distractors.C: RBAC controls which identities may perform actions; it does not restrict which regions a resource may use.
distractors.D: A resource lock prevents deletion or modification of existing resources; it does not restrict allowed regions.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Enforce what can be deployed / allowed config' = Azure Policy.

references: Azure Policy

questions.stem: An Azure Policy must stop anyone from creating a disallowed VM size at deployment time. Which policy effect achieves this?

explanation.correct: The Deny effect blocks a non-compliant resource request, preventing the disallowed VM size from being created.

distractors.A: Append adds fields to a resource; it does not block a disallowed size.
distractors.B: The Audit effect only flags non-compliance in reports; it still allows the resource to be created.
distractors.C: Disabled turns the policy off, so it would enforce nothing.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Block or prevent non-compliant creation' = Deny effect.

references: Azure Policy

questions.stem: A team member should be allowed to manage virtual machines but not networking resources. Which Azure feature grants this scoped permission?

explanation.correct: Azure role-based access control (RBAC) assigns roles at a scope to control who can perform which actions, so you can grant VM management without networking rights.

distractors.A: Microsoft Purview is for data governance, not Azure permission assignment.
distractors.B: A resource lock prevents deletion or changes for everyone; it does not grant per-user permissions.
distractors.D: Azure Policy governs what resource configurations are allowed, not which users may perform actions.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Who can do what' = RBAC; 'what is allowed' = Policy.

references: Azure RBAC

questions.stem: An admin wants to protect a critical resource from accidental deletion while still allowing its settings to be changed. Which lock should they apply?

explanation.correct: A CanNotDelete lock lets authorized users read and modify a resource but blocks its deletion, protecting against accidental removal.

distractors.A: A ReadOnly lock would also block the configuration changes the admin wants to keep allowing.
distractors.B: An Azure Policy Deny governs resource properties at creation or update; it is not the tool for delete-protecting one specific resource.
distractors.D: A Reader role limits a user to viewing; it does not place deletion protection on the resource for everyone.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Prevent deletion but allow edits' = CanNotDelete lock.

references: Azure resource locks

questions.stem: A finished resource must not be modified or deleted by anyone, though it can still be viewed. Which resource lock enforces this?

explanation.correct: A ReadOnly lock allows users to read a resource but prevents all modifications and deletions, even by administrators.

distractors.B: The Audit policy effect only reports non-compliance; it does not block changes or deletions.
distractors.C: The Contributor role grants broad change permissions, the opposite of locking the resource.
distractors.D: A CanNotDelete lock still permits modifications, so it does not fully protect the resource from changes.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'No changes and no deletion, read-only' = ReadOnly lock.

references: Azure resource locks

questions.stem: A business-critical storage account was deleted by mistake last quarter. Which control best prevents that specific resource from being deleted again?

options.text: A resource lock set to CanNotDelete
An Azure Policy with a Deny effect

explanation.correct: A resource lock directly protects a specific existing resource from deletion regardless of a user's RBAC permissions, which fits the accidental-deletion scenario.

distractors.A: A Reader role limits what one identity can do but does not stop other privileged users from deleting the resource.
distractors.C: A budget alert concerns spending, not deletion protection.
distractors.D: Azure Policy Deny evaluates resource properties on create or update to enforce standards; it is not designed to delete-protect one named resource.

explanation.exam_pattern: Protect a specific resource from deletion = resource lock, not Policy.

references: Azure resource locks

questions.stem: A company needs to discover, catalog, and classify sensitive data spread across on-premises, multicloud, and SaaS sources. Which Microsoft solution is designed for this?

explanation.correct: Microsoft Purview is a unified data governance solution that discovers, catalogs, maps, and classifies data assets across on-premises, multicloud, and SaaS estates.

distractors.A: The Service Trust Portal hosts Microsoft's compliance documents; it does not govern your data.
distractors.C: Azure Monitor collects telemetry from resources; it does not catalog or classify data.
distractors.D: Azure Policy enforces configuration rules on Azure resources, not data discovery or classification.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Govern or classify data across the estate' = Microsoft Purview.

references: Microsoft Purview

questions.stem: An auditor asks for Microsoft's independent audit reports and compliance certifications, such as SOC and ISO, for Azure. Where can these be obtained?

explanation.correct: The Service Trust Portal is Microsoft's hub for audit reports, certifications, and compliance documentation (such as SOC and ISO) covering its cloud services.

distractors.A: The Azure Policy compliance view shows whether your own resources meet your policies, not Microsoft's third-party audit reports.
distractors.C: Advisor gives best-practice recommendations, not audit documents.
distractors.D: Microsoft Purview governs your data; it does not supply Microsoft's compliance certifications.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Download Microsoft's audit/compliance reports' = Service Trust Portal.

references: Service Trust Portal

questions.stem: An external auditor must view resources in a subscription but change nothing. Which approach best grants that access to the auditor specifically?

options.text: Give the auditor the Owner role
Apply a ReadOnly lock to the subscription
Assign the auditor the RBAC Reader role

explanation.correct: The Reader RBAC role grants view-only access to a specific identity, which is exactly how to let one auditor see resources without making changes.

distractors.A: An Azure Policy Deny restricts resource configurations, not a user's read access.
distractors.B: The Owner role grants full control, far more than view-only.
distractors.C: A ReadOnly lock blocks changes for everyone, including administrators; it is not a way to grant one person scoped view access.

explanation.exam_pattern: Per-user view-only access = RBAC Reader; locks are not per-user.

references: Azure RBAC

questions.stem: A governance team must apply the same tagging policy consistently across twenty Azure subscriptions at once. Where should the policy be assigned?

options.text: At a management group containing the subscriptions

explanation.correct: Management groups sit above subscriptions and let you assign a policy once so it is inherited by all contained subscriptions, enforcing governance at scale.

distractors.A: Assigning to each resource group individually is error-prone and does not scale to twenty subscriptions.
distractors.B: Assigning to one resource applies nowhere else; it does not cover many subscriptions.
distractors.C: The Pricing Calculator estimates cost; it does not assign policies.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Apply governance across many subscriptions' = management groups.

references: Azure management groups

questions.stem: A team wants to identify resources that lack a required tag without blocking anyone from deploying them. Which Azure Policy effect should they use?

explanation.correct: The Audit effect records non-compliant resources in compliance reports while still allowing them to be created, which fits a report-only goal.

distractors.A: The Deny effect would block deployments, which the team explicitly wants to avoid.
distractors.B: A resource lock prevents deletion or changes; it does not report missing tags.
distractors.D: Append adds a value to a resource rather than reporting non-compliance.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Report non-compliance but do not block' = Audit effect.

references: Azure Policy

questions.stem: After assigning several policies, a cloud team wants to see which of their own Azure resources currently violate those rules. Where do they look?

explanation.correct: Azure Policy includes a compliance view that reports which of your resources are compliant or non-compliant with the policies you assigned.

distractors.A: The Service Trust Portal shows Microsoft's own compliance certifications, not the compliance state of your resources.
distractors.C: The TCO Calculator compares costs; it has no compliance reporting.
distractors.D: Microsoft Purview governs data assets; it does not report Azure Policy compliance.

explanation.exam_pattern: Your resources' compliance = Azure Policy; Microsoft's audits = Service Trust Portal.

references: Azure Policy

questions.stem: Which TWO statements correctly describe the division of responsibility between Azure Policy and Azure RBAC? Select two.

options.text: Azure Policy governs what resource configurations are allowed
Azure RBAC defines which VM sizes may be deployed
Azure Policy decides which users can sign in
Azure RBAC governs which identities may perform actions

explanation.correct: Azure Policy enforces rules about allowed resource configurations (the 'what'), while RBAC controls which users or identities can perform which actions (the 'who'); the two work together.

distractors.B: Allowed VM sizes are enforced by Azure Policy, not by RBAC.
distractors.C: User sign-in and identity are handled by Microsoft Entra ID, not Azure Policy.

explanation.exam_pattern: Policy = what is allowed; RBAC = who can act.

references: Azure Policy
Azure RBAC

questions.stem: A new administrator prefers a visual, point-and-click web interface to create and manage Azure resources. Which management option suits them best?

explanation.correct: The Azure portal is a web-based graphical console for creating, configuring, and managing Azure resources without writing commands.

distractors.A: Azure PowerShell uses scripted cmdlets rather than a graphical interface.
distractors.C: ARM templates are code files for automated deployment, not an interactive interface.
distractors.D: Azure CLI is a text command-line tool, not a point-and-click GUI.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Visual / point-and-click management' = Azure portal.

references: Azure portal

questions.stem: An engineer needs to run a few Azure commands from a borrowed laptop with nothing installed, using a browser-based shell that is already authenticated. What fits?

explanation.correct: Azure Cloud Shell is a browser-based, pre-authenticated shell (Bash or PowerShell) available in the portal, so no local installation is required.

distractors.B: Advisor provides recommendations; it is not a command shell.
distractors.C: Installing Azure CLI locally requires setup on the machine, which the borrowed-laptop scenario rules out.
distractors.D: An ARM template is a deployment file, not an interactive shell.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Browser shell, nothing to install, already signed in' = Cloud Shell.

references: Azure Cloud Shell

questions.stem: A cross-platform team wants to script Azure management using concise commands that all begin with 'az'. Which tool are they describing?

explanation.correct: Azure CLI is a cross-platform command-line tool whose commands start with 'az', used for scripting and automating Azure management.

distractors.B: The Azure portal is a graphical interface, not an 'az' command tool.
distractors.C: Azure PowerShell uses verb-noun cmdlets such as Get-AzVM, not 'az' commands.
distractors.D: Bicep is a declarative infrastructure-as-code language, not an interactive command tool.

explanation.exam_pattern: Commands beginning with 'az' = Azure CLI.

references: Azure CLI

questions.stem: A Windows-focused administrator wants to automate Azure tasks using verb-noun cmdlets like Get-AzVM from the Az module. Which tool is this?

explanation.correct: Azure PowerShell provides the Az module of cmdlets (such as Get-AzVM) for scripting and automating Azure management, popular with PowerShell users.

distractors.A: ARM templates are declarative JSON files, not interactive cmdlets.
distractors.C: Azure CLI uses 'az' commands, not PowerShell cmdlets.
distractors.D: Azure Monitor is a monitoring service, not a scripting tool.

explanation.exam_pattern: Az module verb-noun cmdlets = Azure PowerShell.

references: Azure PowerShell

questions.stem: A team must deploy the same multi-resource environment identically in several subscriptions, repeatedly and without manual steps. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Build each environment by hand in the portal

explanation.correct: ARM templates are declarative JSON files that define infrastructure as code, enabling repeatable, consistent, automated deployments across subscriptions.

distractors.A: Advisor provides recommendations; it does not deploy environments.
distractors.B: Building by hand in the portal is manual and error-prone, producing inconsistent environments.
distractors.D: Service Health reports Azure service status; it does not deploy resources.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Repeatable, identical, automated deployment' = IaC templates.

references: Azure Resource Manager templates

questions.stem: Engineers find their ARM JSON templates verbose and want a cleaner, purpose-built language that still compiles down to ARM. What should they adopt?

explanation.correct: Bicep is a domain-specific language with simpler, more readable syntax that transpiles to ARM templates, giving the same declarative deployments with less verbosity.

distractors.A: Imperative CLI scripts are a different style and do not provide the declarative template model the team wants.
distractors.B: Writing more ARM JSON keeps the very verbosity the team is trying to escape.
distractors.D: The portal is manual and graphical, not a cleaner IaC authoring language.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Cleaner, readable IaC that compiles to ARM' = Bicep.

references: Bicep

questions.stem: A team wants personalized recommendations to improve the security, reliability, performance, and cost of their existing Azure resources. Which service provides these?

explanation.correct: Azure Advisor analyzes your resources and gives personalized best-practice recommendations across cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance.

distractors.A: Azure Policy enforces configuration rules; it does not recommend improvements.
distractors.B: Service Health reports Azure service outages and maintenance, not optimization recommendations.
distractors.C: Azure Monitor collects and analyzes telemetry; it does not itself produce the curated best-practice recommendations Advisor does.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Personalized best-practice recommendations' = Azure Advisor.

references: Azure Advisor

questions.stem: An operations team wants to collect CPU and memory metrics from their VMs and raise an alert when a VM is overloaded. Which service do they use?

explanation.correct: Azure Monitor collects metrics and logs (telemetry) from resources and can trigger alerts, such as when a VM's CPU exceeds a threshold.

distractors.A: Advisor gives recommendations; it is not the telemetry-collection and alerting engine.
distractors.B: Microsoft Purview governs data; it does not monitor VM performance.
distractors.C: The Service Trust Portal hosts compliance documents, not resource metrics.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Collect metrics/logs and alert on resources' = Azure Monitor.

references: Azure Monitor

questions.stem: An engineer wants to run queries across collected log data from many resources using a query language in a central workspace. Which Azure Monitor feature is this?

explanation.correct: Log Analytics is the Azure Monitor tool for running queries (using KQL) against log data stored in a Log Analytics workspace.

distractors.A: Service Health reports Azure service status, not your log queries.
distractors.B: Application Insights focuses on monitoring applications, not general cross-resource log querying.
distractors.C: Advisor provides recommendations, not a log query experience.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Query collected logs in a workspace' = Log Analytics.

references: Azure Monitor Log Analytics

questions.stem: A developer wants to monitor a live web application's response times, request failures, and availability from the user's perspective. Which tool fits?

explanation.correct: Application Insights is the Azure Monitor application performance management feature that tracks a live app's requests, failures, dependencies, and availability.

distractors.A: Service Health reports Azure platform status, not your application's performance.
distractors.B: Azure Policy enforces resource rules; it does not monitor applications.
distractors.C: Log Analytics queries collected logs generally; Application Insights is the purpose-built app performance tool for this scenario.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Monitor a live app's performance/availability' = Application Insights.

references: Azure Monitor Application Insights

questions.stem: An operations team needs to know whether an ongoing Azure platform outage or planned maintenance is affecting the services they use. Which tool shows this?

explanation.correct: Azure Service Health gives a personalized view of Azure service issues, planned maintenance, and health advisories affecting the resources and regions you use.

distractors.B: Application Insights monitors your application, not Azure platform health.
distractors.C: Advisor provides optimization recommendations, not platform outage status.
distractors.D: Cost Management tracks spending, not service outages.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Is an Azure outage/maintenance affecting me?' = Service Health.

references: Azure Service Health

questions.stem: Azure flags that a consistently underused VM should be resized to save money. Which service surfaces this specific cost-optimization recommendation?

explanation.correct: Azure Advisor's cost recommendations identify underutilized resources and advise actions such as resizing or shutting down a VM to save money.

distractors.A: A resource lock prevents deletion or changes; it does not recommend resizing.
distractors.C: Azure Monitor can show the underlying utilization metrics, but the actionable right-size recommendation is produced by Advisor.
distractors.D: Service Health reports Azure outages and maintenance, not cost recommendations.

explanation.exam_pattern: Actionable right-size/cost recommendation = Advisor (Monitor shows raw metrics).

references: Azure Advisor

questions.stem: An administrator wants to be notified only when Microsoft reports an Azure service outage, not when a VM's own CPU spikes. Which alert should they set up?

explanation.correct: Service Health alerts notify you about Azure platform issues such as outages, maintenance, and advisories affecting your services.

distractors.A: An Application Insights web test checks application availability, not Azure platform outages.
distractors.C: An Azure Monitor metric alert fires on resource metrics like CPU, which is exactly what the administrator wants to exclude.
distractors.D: A budget alert concerns spending, not service outages.

explanation.exam_pattern: Notification about Azure platform outages = Service Health alert.

references: Azure Service Health

questions.stem: Which TWO options let you define Azure infrastructure as code for automated, repeatable deployments? Select two.

explanation.correct: ARM templates (declarative JSON) and Bicep (a cleaner language that compiles to ARM) are both infrastructure-as-code options for repeatable, automated Azure deployments.

distractors.C: Azure Service Health reports Azure service status; it is not an infrastructure-as-code tool.
distractors.D: Azure Advisor provides best-practice recommendations; it does not define or deploy infrastructure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Azure IaC = ARM templates and Bicep.

references: Azure Resource Manager templates
Bicep
